title: Parse the load fallback with the segmented parser, projectors kept
head: 0aba66119a
what: When the fast parser rejects saved text, the fallback now types it in as top-level pieces of at least 100 characters, each into a fresh zipper, joined and re-grouted once, instead of character by character; projector pins are kept.
changes: Yes, on the fallback path (saved programs with an unfinished form or a concave hole, share links, the CLI's tutorial decoding): a piece is parsed without its left context.
mechanism: Parser.to_zipper_segmented splits where the caret is at top level, outside any token, with no missing shards, just after whitespace (Parser.re:81-85). The join is re-grouted (Parser.re:158), never remolded, and the caller does not remold afterwards.
argument: The PR checks the printed text against the character-by-character parser on 128 inputs, and keeps projector ids across the split (sound).
assumes: That a piece's first token is molded the same way without what precedes it. That is false for tokens whose mold depends on their left neighbour.
risk: - (binary or unary) and ( (application or parentheses) are molded by their left neighbour, and an ascription's right side switches to types. If a split lands just after an operand, as when 100 characters end inside x in a top-level x - y, the next piece starts in a concave context: - becomes unary minus and the join gets a hole, so aaa…a - b loads as aaa…a ¿ -b, and f (b) as f ¿ (b). Splits also happen right after a comment's closing #. Rare per program, but silent at load, and written back on the next save. Found by reading the code; a test to confirm it is the first step below.
tests_have: Parser.Segmented compares 5 files and a prose paragraph with the character-by-character parser, by printed text.
tests_missing: The constructed cases above, against the character-by-character parser.
A sweep of split positions: each corpus program with 0 to 99 characters of padding in front, so every top-level space becomes a split point at some offset.
Fallback-shaped inputs (an unfinished form at the end, concave holes), compared as terms, not only printed text.
A likely fix, not yet tried: remold the joined zipper once before the final re-grout.

title: Load text about 2.5× faster: whole tokens, one re-grout
head: b4e3914b03
what: Loading types each run of operand or operator characters in as one insertion and re-grouts once at the end, not after every character; rescanning returns its own argument when nothing changed, tested by identity; a carriage return reads as a newline.
changes: Designed not to, and no case found by reading, except the line-ending change, which changes the parse on purpose for text with \r (loading, the paste fallback, splice paste).
mechanism: to_zipper ~by_run; take_run stops where typing would stop extending a token; one remold_regrout at the end; Siblings.rescan returns its argument unchanged when nothing converted.
argument: The identity check is exactly the old structural one: rescanning alters a piece only at a conversion, which it flags. Whole-token runs: the operand and operator character classes are disjoint and no token spans both, and insertion still merges with its left neighbour. One re-grout: remolding skips grout and passes shapes through, so molds cannot depend on grout, and the final pass puts the same 0 or 1 grout at each junction.
assumes: That insertion's choices do not depend on grout or on per-prefix side effects (three places in Insert read grout, for ids, a suppressed space and the caret, none for the term).
risk: A hole's place relative to a neighbouring space may differ (text and layout, not the term). A lone \r inside a string or comment now splits it into fragments (dev dropped it silently); rare and loud. CRLF text, which loaded with a hole on every line, now loads right. #2610 and #2614 both rewrite the same fallback: merging both needs a choice.
tests_have: Parser.LoadPath (6 tests); 386 parse tests; a structural comparison on 72 programs, run once offline.
tests_missing: In CI: whole-token runs on against off, ids erased, over the corpus and fallback-shaped inputs (prose, hole-heavy text, unfinished endings, x+-1, >>=, 1.5e-3, Unicode names, strings and comments with spaces).

title: MapPiece keeps unchanged pieces as the same objects
head: 04e1c6c362
what: Mapping over a segment returns the original object wherever nothing under it changed.
changes: No: the output is structurally equal to before; only sharing differs.
mechanism: Identity checks (===) on each piece and tile; the updater is applied piece by piece and then recursed into, where the old code applied it to a whole level first: the same calls in a different order.
argument: If every piece maps to itself the output is element for element the input, so returning the input is equivalent. All five callers on dev are pure or order-independent.
assumes: That updaters are pure, or at least do not depend on call order.
risk: A future updater that depends on order would break. It makes identity-keyed caches hit after projector updates; on #2635 that switches on incremental term-building reuse, which is sound only if an item's term depends on nothing outside its own pieces (a question for #2635's review).
tests_have: MapPieceIdentity: a no-op update returns the same segment, and the top-level prefix is kept (both fail without the change).
tests_missing: A property test: new against old, structurally, for random pure updaters; identity checked at depth.

title: Measuring the font no longer scrolls the editor to the caret
head: 86bdda9d0c
what: Storing the measured font no longer asks the editor to scroll the caret into view.
changes: No. Only the scroll flag flips; nothing recalculated before or after.
argument: The metrics are stored exactly as before, and the update never triggered a recalculation; the flag only decides whether the caret is scrolled into view after drawing.
risk: User-visible and deliberate: after a zoom or a web font settling, the caret is no longer brought back into view. The reveal at startup still happens.

short: worker at load, no false timeout
title: Eval worker in Firefox: start it at load, and do not time out a reply that is queued
head: 9de67fdf30
what: The eval worker starts with the page; a deadline timer that fires more than 250 ms late waits another 500 ms and checks again instead of declaring a timeout.
changes: No: only whether and when the page gives up. What is sent, and which replies are accepted (the latest request id), is unchanged; a spurious "Evaluation timed out" now shows the real result.
mechanism: set_deadline (WorkerClient.re:57-74) re-arms a late timer; the timer reference always holds the latest one, so clearing cancels re-armed timers too.
argument: A fresh worker starts in the same state whenever it is created; replies are matched by request id, so a stale one is dropped.
assumes: That a worker message already queued runs before a 500 ms timer set after it (not guaranteed by the spec; if not, the timer decides as before).
risk: The evaluation deadline is no longer a fixed 20 s: in a hidden tab, timers run late and re-arm indefinitely, so a runaway evaluation keeps a core busy until the tab is visible. That delays a timeout message; it never shows a wrong result.
tests_missing: set_deadline against a fake clock: fires when on time, re-arms when late, clearing cancels a re-armed timer.
